Valenciennes
va-lahn-see-EN
n. (the Hainaut town that held out for the Reformed in 1566, was stormed in 1567, and where Guido de Bres was hanged)
French Valenciennes, from a Gallo-Roman estate name, perhaps of the emperor Valentinian; the town stands on the Scheldt in Hainaut.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Valenciennes is the town that made the first armed stand of the Dutch Reformation and lost it. Its Reformed congregation was among the oldest and boldest in the Walloon provinces; in 1562 the townspeople rescued two ministers from the stake and the psalm-singing processions that followed, the chanteries, were treated by the government as open rebellion. After the image-breaking of August 1566 the Reformed took effective control of the town, held public worship, and when the regent demanded a royal garrison in December they refused to admit it. Valenciennes was besieged through the winter, bombarded, and stormed on 23 March 1567, after which the executions began. Guido de Bres, who had come into the town to serve and strengthen the congregation during the siege, was captured in flight, imprisoned at Tournai and Valenciennes, examined at length, and hanged in the marketplace on 31 May 1567 with his fellow minister Peregrin de la Grange. His prison letters to his wife, his mother and his congregation were printed and circulated widely. The dictionary enters Valenciennes because the author of the Belgic Confession died there, and because a town that refused a garrison in December was storming distance from a Spanish army in March.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bombardment as an attack with shells; to storm as to assault and take by force; a marketplace as the place of public sale; and an epistle as a letter written and sent.

expand to see more

BOMBARDMENT, n. An attack with bombs; the act of throwing bombs into a town, fort or ship.

STORM, v. To attack; to assault; to attempt to take by open force, as a fort or fortified town.

MARKETPLACE, n. The place where provisions or goods are exposed for sale; a public place in a town.

EPISTLE, n. A writing, directed or sent to a person or persons; a letter; a letter missive.

SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or for the execution of a criminal.

Modern Corruption

Hainaut town whose Reformed congregation refused a royal garrison in 1566, was stormed in March 1567, and where Guido de Bres was hanged on 31 May 1567.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the confusing of a congregation's cause with a town's defences. Valenciennes had the better doctrine and the worse walls, and the dictionary does not pretend the refusal of the garrison was a wise act; it was a brave one made by men who had already seen their ministers taken to the stake, and it ended in a storm, a sack and a scaffold. What is not in doubt is the manner of the dying. De Bres went into a besieged town to serve a congregation he could have left, and his own words from the prison are of a piece with the apostle's: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phi 1:21).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pastor's obligation to the flock in the hour when leaving would be reasonable. “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24) is the charge de Bres accepted, and of his ending the plainest word is “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). To the congregation he wrote to from the prison, the promise given to Smyrna applies: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stephanos (G4735), a crown; Greek dromos (G1408), a course, a race; Greek kerdos (G2771), gain.

expand to see more

Greek stephanos (G4735) — a crown, a victor's garland; “I will give thee a crown of life”, Revelation 2:10.

Greek dromos (G1408) — a course, a race run out; “that I might finish my course with joy”, Acts 20:24.

Greek kerdos (G2771) — gain, profit; “to die is gain”, Philippians 1:21.

Greek agon (G73) — a contest, a struggle; “I have fought a good fight”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to guard, to hold fast; “I have kept the faith”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

Usage

"“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phi 1:21) — de Bres's prison letters, printed and circulated."

"“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — hanged in the marketplace, 31 May 1567."

"“be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) — a town stormed on 23 March 1567."
